title: Hooks and lifecycle
description: No-code rules of the form “when this happens in a turn, do that”: events, actions and why a block always wins.

steps.question: An alarm is a write action, and by default the agent sets it silently. But you want it to ask first. You don't write code. How?
steps.answer: Attach a hook: event “Before tool,” condition “Alarm,” action “Require approval.” Hooks are rules on turn events that sit on top of the default rules, with no programming.

steps.text: First, the lifecycle. One agent turn is not a single moment but a chain of phases: think → get ready to call a tool → receive the result → think again, round and round until it answers. Every phase has a “before” and an “after,” and you can step in at those moments.

steps.imagePrompt: A small robot runs laps on a circular track with six checkpoints. At one checkpoint a gate with a stop sign holds back an envelope until a human hand gives a thumbs up.
steps.caption: A hook is a rule on a turn event

steps.definition: A rule of the form “on event X, do Y” that you attach to a phase of the turn. It is declarative: you describe a condition and an action from ready-made blocks instead of writing code.
steps.example: Event “Before tool,” condition “Alarm” → action “Require approval.” Done, with no programming.

steps.text: There are six turn events you can attach a hook to: before the turn and after it, before a tool call and after it, on error, and on completion. Each one is a point where the engine stops and asks: “are there any rules for this moment?”

steps.instruction: Match each event to the moment it fires:

pairs.def: The agent is about to call a tool but hasn't yet

steps.text: What a hook can do. Add an instruction (“answer briefly”), require confirmation before an action, block a tool, stop the whole turn, or simply write the event to a log. A hook's condition is simple: “always” or “only for tools from a list.” There is also an “Allow” action, but it cannot get around the rules: sending anything outside the app and deleting still ask for your “OK,” and any block outweighs it.

steps.caption: Switch rules on and run a turn: see which event fires each one

steps.situation: Two hooks are attached to the “Email” tool: one allows it, the other blocks it.
options: Block it: any block that fires outweighs an allow
Allow it: “Allow” removes both the block and the question
Ask the user which rule to apply
steps.explain: The rule is simple and safe: any block that fires outweighs any allow. There is no “the more important rule wins.”

steps.text: Important: the hook engine is deterministic. The same input always gives the same decision. It calls nothing itself (no model, no tool). It only combines the matching rules into one decision. And what exactly fired is visible in the run log, so you can work it out later.

One more thing: hooks cover not only the turn but also the steps of a structured plan: before a plan step, after it, and when it is blocked. Plans get a lesson of their own. Here, what matters is that the rule mechanism is the same.

Practice. After the lesson, build an agent: Agents → Create agent. Describe in the chat what it should do, and give it the “Alarm” tool (if the Builder doesn't suggest it, tick it in the tools list on the review screen). When the “Review your agent” card appears, open it. In the “Rules (hooks)” section tap “Edit rules” and add a hook: “Before tool,” tick “Alarm” in the condition, and set the action to “Require approval.” Then ask the agent to set an alarm, either in “Try it” on the review screen or in a chat with it after you publish. You will see the “The agent needs your permission” bar, even though setting an alarm normally happens silently. For an agent you have already published, you edit rules the same way: open the agent and tap “Edit.” The builder itself gets a full lesson next.

In short. A hook is a declarative “on a turn event, do an action” rule, with no code. There are six events (before and after the turn, before and after a tool, error, completion). The condition is “always” or “tools from a list.” The actions are: add an instruction, require confirmation, block, stop, write to the log. Hooks work on top of the default rules: “Allow” does not cancel them, any block outweighs an allow, the engine is deterministic, and the log shows what fired.

questions.q: What is a hook in an agent?
options: A no-code rule: on a turn event, do an action
A Kotlin script that the user writes by hand
An Android permission setting for the app
questions.explain: A hook is a rule on a phase of the turn: a condition plus an action from ready-made blocks.

questions.q: A tool has both an allow and a block attached. Which one wins?
options: The block: it outweighs any allow
The allow: it always has priority
Whichever rule was added to the agent last
questions.explain: A single block that fires always outweighs an allow. That is the safe default.

questions.q: What does the hook engine NOT do?
options: Call a tool itself: it only decides, the turn acts
Add an extra instruction to the prompt
Stop the turn or require confirmation
questions.explain: The engine is pure and deterministic: it combines rules into a decision, and the turn itself carries it out.

questions.q: An “Allow” hook is attached to “Email.” Will the agent ask for your “OK” before a message?
options: Yes: the default rule can't be bypassed
No: the hook removes the question
questions.explain: Email goes outside the app, and that always waits for your “OK.” “Allow” does not cancel the default rules.
